job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Esther Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing a master's in cybersecurity in Lisbon and still living with my parents in Almada, so I take the ferry across the river every morning. I have lectures until two, then I do freelance web work for small shops, which pays for my own treats. I use an AI assistant for nearly everything, from code to emails to planning my week. My internship last year was at a bank's security team, where I helped sort out phishing reports.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's helpful, but not the big deal people shout about. I'd tell my classmates it's a better autocomplete, and online I'd probably reply to one or two threads before getting bored. I'd say my parents' generation worries too much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, for me a plateau is fine. Cybersecurity gets busier whenever tools get used more, and attackers use these tools too. My freelance work covers a lot of the small stuff, so I feel pretty covered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, take the bank's offer if it comes, and keep freelancing for a year. I'd keep using the assistant every day but keep a notebook of what it gets wrong. I'd put a bit of money aside for a trip with my brother.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels easy, which is rare. Nothing to fix, nothing to chase.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you keep notes on what the assistant gets wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because security people get hurt by trusting outputs. Last year the assistant suggested a code library that didn't exist, and an attacker could have registered that name. I make a list of its errors and I've found it's weirdly useful for exams.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Any worries at all in the plateau?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money pressure at home, a bit. My dad is a ferry mechanic and the company keeps saying it'll modernise, so I worry about his job. He's fifty-six and wouldn't retrain easily.

say: I'd say AI is a **better autocomplete**, not the big deal people shout about.
I'd tell my parents' generation they **worry too much**.
think: A plateau is fine because **cybersecurity** gets busier whenever tools spread and attackers use them too.
My freelance work covers **small stuff** so I feel covered.
do: Finish the master's and take the **bank's offer** if it comes.
Keep **freelancing** for a year and note the assistant's errors.
feel: I feel **easy**, which is rare, with nothing to fix or chase.
S0.quote: The assistant suggested a code library that didn't exist, and an attacker could have registered that name.
fieldNote: Esther is **secure** and treats AI as an everyday tool she audits.
Her one anchor worry is her father's job at the ferry company.
She keeps an error log of the assistant, a security habit.

steps.text: Take the bank's security team offer if it arrives
Keep freelance web work going for another year
Keep a log of the AI assistant's mistakes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a good time to be young and curious. In the class chat I'd say learn it, test it and break it. On social media I'd share small examples of where it fails, because it helps people be less scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think a lot of junior security tasks, like sorting alerts and writing reports, go to software. But attackers get these tools too, so the defenders need people who can think like them. I think I'm well placed, but not safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start building my own small tools with the assistant, for example one that sorts phishing reports faster than I did at the bank. I'd enter two capture-the-flag competitions and apply for the bank's graduate program early. I'd also teach my dad how to spot scam messages, because he's already received two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels exciting. A little tiring, because everything speeds up and I want to keep pace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is it about attackers that worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That they only need to be right once. A scammer can send a million perfect messages at no cost. Defenders have to answer every one of them. I find that very motivating, but it's not fair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the bank cuts junior analysts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd go to a security start-up, which are smaller and hire people who can build things. Honestly I like start-ups better, I get bored in big teams. My freelancing is useful too, because it shows I can work without a manager.

say: I'd say learn it, test it and **break it**.
I'd share small examples of where it **fails** so people are less scared.
think: Many junior security tasks like sorting alerts go to **software**, but defenders still need people who think like attackers.
do: Build my own small tool with the assistant that sorts **phishing reports** faster.
Enter two **capture-the-flag** competitions and apply for the bank's graduate programme early.
feel: I feel **excited**, and a little tired because everything speeds up.
S1.quote: A scammer can send a million perfect messages at no cost. Defenders have to answer every one of them.
fieldNote: Esther is **calm** because her skills are on the building side and she has options.
She enjoys the attacker-defender arms race.
Teaching her dad about scams shows how she connects work to family.

steps.text: Build a phishing report sorting tool using the AI assistant
Enter two capture-the-flag security competitions this year
Apply early to the bank's graduate programme
Teach my dad to spot scam messages

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is too quick for anyone to be fair. I'd say publicly that banks and governments need transition plans, and that cybersecurity will be a front line. I'd tell classmates to ignore advice to wait and to start earning now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm anxious. By 2028 the junior security analyst roles I'm aiming at are probably automated, and so is most of the software work I freelance on. I'd be 26 with a master's and a chat assistant that does my job for nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, skip the planned break and take the first real job I can get, ideally in a bank or the government, where cybersecurity rules need people to sign things off. I'd keep every freelance client and ask them for referrals. I'd also pay off nothing early and keep cash, since I'd need flexibility.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a countdown. I'm not frozen, but I check the news too often.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your parents do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mother works in a school canteen, so her job holds longer. My dad is on the ferry, and I'd expect software to manage the schedules even if the engines still need a mechanic. I'd tell them to cut spending now and keep the savings my grandmother left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd regret?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not having started earlier on the human side of security: the policy, the audits, the people who decide. The technical side is the part that machines learn fastest, so I'd put more effort into persuasion and trust.

say: I'd say banks and governments need **transition plans** and security will be a front line.
I'd tell classmates **not to wait** and to start earning now.
think: Junior security analyst roles and the freelance **software work** are probably automated by 2028.
The **human side** of security, like audits and policy, is where I should have started earlier.
do: Take the **first real job** I can get, ideally at a bank or in government.
Keep every **freelance client**, ask for referrals and hold cash for flexibility.
feel: I feel a **countdown**, not frozen, but I check the news too often.
S2.quote: The technical side is the part that machines learn fastest, so I'd put more effort into persuasion and trust.
fieldNote: Esther is **anxious** but active; she converts worry into job moves and referrals.
She identifies the human side of security as the area machines learn last.
Her parents' jobs differ in exposure, and she reasons about each.

steps.text: Take the first real security job at a bank or ministry
Ask every freelance client for two referrals this month
Study audit and policy skills alongside the technical master's
Ask my parents to cut spending and protect savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough to adjust, and I'd say so. I'd say publicly that governments should fund retraining in trust-based work like audits and security. I'd tell friends to try to be one of the people who checks AI, not one who competes with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm uneasy but optimistic. By 2031 I'd have three years in the field and I'd have made friends who hire. The thinking tasks go, but the person who knows what to ask and what to distrust is still valuable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the master's, join a bank or consulting firm, and take a security audit certificate. I'd mentor interns, because teaching forces me to learn. I'd save about a fifth of my pay and start learning about regulation, because every new AI rule creates work for someone who can read it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels okay. A good amount of time to prepare, though I'd probably still feel rushed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the extra time change compared to two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'd take any job. With five I'd pick one with a mentor who is good, even if the pay is lower. A bad first boss costs more than a small pay difference.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if your dad's ferry company cut his job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move him into a part-time job with the maintenance firm I know through my uncle. I'd also pay for a short course for him in electric engines, since the fleet is going electric anyway. He'd grumble and then enjoy it.

say: I'd say governments should fund retraining in **trust-based work** like audits and security.
I'd tell friends to be someone who **checks** AI, not competes with it.
think: By 2031 I'd have three years in the field and **friends who hire**.
Someone who knows what to **distrust** is still valuable.
do: Join a bank or consulting firm and take a **security audit** certificate.
Mentor interns and save a **fifth** of my pay.
feel: I feel **okay**, with good time to prepare but still a bit rushed.
S3.quote: With two years I'd take any job. With five I'd pick one with a mentor who is good, even if the pay is lower.
fieldNote: Esther's **mentor-first** logic changes with the longer horizon.
She plans concrete help for her father's job, linking family and work.
She sees regulation as a job creator.

steps.text: Join a bank audit team with a strong mentor
Earn a security audit certificate in the first year
Save a fifth of my pay from the first month
Pay for my dad's short electric engine course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is generous. I'd say we should use it to set rules for the machines and make sure everyone can use them. I'd tell friends to enjoy their twenties, but make one move a year toward something sturdy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel good. By 2036 I'd be 34, maybe leading a small security team, and I'd have lived through the transition as an insider. The robots for hands-on jobs come around 2039, which is a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work at a bank for four years, then try a start-up with a friend from my master's. I'd keep using the assistant daily, but my real focus would be the human side: risk, audit, regulation. I'd buy a small flat in Almada near my parents and still take ferries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels light, like a long weekend ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would make this world go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the rules don't arrive and a few firms own everything. I'm okay with change, but I don't like the idea of an unaccountable system running things. That's the thing I'd vote about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want in ten years that you don't have now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A team that trusts me and a sister or brother who's finished their studies. And maybe a dog. I'd say that's a perfectly sensible plan for 2036.

say: I'd say we should use the decade to set **rules** and let everyone use the tools.
I'd tell friends to make **one move a year** toward something sturdy.
think: By 2036 I'd be 34, maybe leading a small **security team**.
The danger is a few firms owning everything with **no accountability**.
do: Work four years at a bank, then try a **start-up** with a friend.
Buy a small **flat** in Almada near my parents.
feel: I feel **light**, like a long weekend ahead.
S4.quote: I'm okay with change, but I don't like the idea of an unaccountable system running things.
fieldNote: Esther's calm at ten years comes from **insider** status and gradual planning.
Her one civic worry is unaccountable systems controlled by a few firms.
Humour and small personal goals soften the plan.

steps.text: Work four years at a bank security team, then co-found a start-up
Buy a small flat in Almada near my parents
Vote for rules that hold AI companies accountable

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd have no time to build a track record. What would help is a clear route into security jobs for new graduates, and rules that make companies explain when AI is making a decision. A bit of income support in a bad year would take the edge off, too.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd add that I'm not as fearless as people think, even if I use AI every day. Using a tool and trusting it are different things, and I'd like people to hear that.

headlineQuote: Using a tool and trusting it are different things, and I'd like people to hear that.
portrait: Esther is 24, doing a **cybersecurity** master's in Lisbon and living with her parents in Almada.
She uses AI every day but logs its **mistakes**, because trust and use are different things.
Her centre outlook is pragmatic and she values rules that keep systems accountable.
In the two-year world she turns anxious and takes the **first real job** she can get.
With five or ten years she picks mentors, certificates and a **start-up** plan.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** world, because she would have no time to build a track record.
whatWouldHelp: A clear route into **security jobs** for new graduates and rules that make firms explain AI decisions.
